name: Scalp flaps

lead: A scalp flap relocates a patch of hair-bearing scalp, with its blood supply intact, to cover a nearby area that has lost skin or hair. It is a reconstructive surgery staple used after burns, tumour removal and trauma.
People interested in it for looks see it as a way to cover scarred or hairless areas with their own hair-bearing skin, often combined with tissue expansion or hair transplants.

paras: The surgeon designs a flap, often a rotation flap, that shifts neighbouring scalp skin into the defect. Pre-expansion with an implant can stretch skin first. Hair-sparing incision planning aims at a natural result [1][4][5].

As with any surgery: scarring, healing problems and anaesthesia risks. Case reports describe specific complications such as bulldog scalp syndrome and sunken flap syndrome after skull surgery [2][7]. Performed by qualified surgeons.

chain: Nearby scalp skin is moved on its own blood supply
Bald or scarred area is covered with hair-bearing skin
angle.text: Scalp flaps move hair-bearing skin over areas that have lost hair or skin, such as burn scars or surgical defects. Surgeons choose the flap design and hair-sparing approach to keep the result looking natural [4][5].

lead: A scalp flap is a section of scalp skin, with its blood supply left attached, that a surgeon moves to cover a nearby area that has lost skin or hair. Because the scalp is tight and has little give, surgeons plan flaps carefully, and rotation flaps are described as the main workhorses of scalp reconstruction [1]. For appearance, the goal is a covered defect with the surrounding hair-bearing scalp kept in a natural pattern.

In appearance terms, flaps are used to restore coverage after burns, tumour removal or injury, and to keep incisions within or behind the hairline. Reconstruction reviews describe pairing flaps with tissue expansion and hair transplants to refine the final aesthetic result. Surgical planning papers describe hair-sparing techniques and flap design as ways to reach a good cosmetic outcome.
Most published material comes from reconstructive, neurosurgical and ENT surgery rather than cosmetic surgery, and it describes the technique in those settings.
infobox: Covering scalp defects, scars and burn alopecia
Rotation flaps, advancement flaps, pre-expanded flaps

paras: The scalp's anatomy largely decides which parts can be moved, and large shifts of skin are often needed to close a defect [1]. A systematic approach to scalp defects covers grafts and flaps, and describes how flap selection, design and execution are planned.

Flaps are also used in neurosurgery, where incisions are shaped to spare hair and protect the underlying tissues. Related flap types, such as pericranial flaps, are used in skull base reconstruction [2].

Burn alopecia, the hair loss that follows scalp burns, has been treated with surgical methods since at least the 1970s. Tissue expansion, in which an implant stretches nearby scalp skin before a flap is moved, has been used to eliminate large scalp defects [3], and a registered trial studied how to choose rectangular expanders for burn scars and scalp wounds [4]. A 2026 randomized comparison looked at pre-expanded fronto-scalp flaps combined with botulinum toxin and laser therapy for large craniofacial defects [5].

Flap surgery carries the usual surgical risks. Case reports describe unusual appearance-related complications such as bulldog scalp syndrome [6]. In patients who have had part of the skull removed, the scalp flap can sink inward and neurological symptoms have been reported, which improved after cranioplasty in a small case series [7][8].

Evidence is mostly narrative reviews and case series of reconstructive surgery [1]. Registered studies include a completed 19-patient expander study in burn scars and scalp wounds [4] and a 72-patient trial of an external skull prosthesis to prevent sunken flap syndrome [9]. No trials were found that study scalp flaps specifically for cosmetic hair restoration.

timeline.event: Burn alopecia treatment is described in plastic surgery literature.
Skin expansion is reported as a way to remove large scalp defects [3].
A review describes rotation flaps as the main scalp reconstruction technique [1].
A systematic approach to scalp defect reconstruction is published.
